## Julius

Yes — this can make cryptographic sense, but the clean way to think about it is:

•           **identity keys** prove _who_ is acting

•           **group encryption keys** control _who can read messages_

•           **admin authorization keys** control _who is allowed to change membership or policy_

The main thing I would change in your idea is this:

## The biggest design correction

You probably **do not want users sharing their master private key**.

A private master key should normally stay on that user’s device forever. If Jane shares her master private key, then whoever gets it can permanently impersonate her. You said you are not worried about that for now, but from a protocol-design perspective it is still better to avoid building around shared private keys.

Instead, use this model:

•           Each user has a long-term **identity keypair**

–          private identity key stays secret

–          public identity key is known to the group

•           The group chat has a **group encryption state**

–          one current group key per epoch

•           The admin has an **admin signing key**

–          used to authorize membership changes, rekeys, kicks, policy changes

That gives you exactly what you want: - members can send/read normal messages - members **cannot** invite or add people by themselves unless the protocol allows it - admin approval can be made cryptographically mandatory

---

## A practical mental model

Think of your system as having **three layers**.

### 1. User identity layer

Each participant has:

•           IK_priv = identity private key

•           IK_pub = identity public key

Use this for: - signing messages - proving who requested an action - authenticating devices/users

Good simple choices: - **Ed25519** for signatures - **X25519** for key agreement

These are modern, simple, fast, and widely used.

---

### 2. Group membership and encryption layer

The group chat itself has:

•           GroupID

•           Epoch

•           GK_epoch = current group encryption key for that epoch

Use this for: - encrypting chat messages - rotating keys after joins/kicks - controlling who can read messages

Good simple choice: - **XChaCha20-Poly1305** or **AES-256-GCM** for message encryption - If you want easier nonce safety in distributed systems, **XChaCha20-Poly1305** is very attractive

Each message in the queue should include something like:

•           group id

•           epoch number

•           sender id

•           message sequence id

•           ciphertext

•           sender signature

Since your queue is append-only and keeps old messages, the **epoch number is critical**.

Why: - old members can still decrypt old epochs they were part of - kicked members should **not** decrypt future epochs - new members should generally **not** decrypt old epochs unless you explicitly give them old keys

That is exactly how “keep messages forever but still support removal” is usually handled.

---

### 3. Admin authorization layer

Bob, the admin, has:

•           Admin_priv

•           Admin_pub

Use this key only for admin-authorized actions:

•           add member

•           approve invite

•           kick member

•           rotate group key

•           change permissions

•           freeze queue

•           reset group cryptography

This is the key that enforces: > some actions cannot happen without Bob’s permission

That is the right role for the admin key.

---

## The core rule you want

You said:

If Jane wanted to invite John, I want there to be a cryptographic function to make it not possible for her to do so without Bob’s permission.

Yes. The clean way is:

## Use signed admin certificates for membership changes

A new member becomes valid **only if there is an admin-signed membership event** in the queue.

So Jane can do at most:

•           create an invite request

•           nominate John

•           maybe encrypt some onboarding data for John

But John is **not actually a member** unless Bob signs an approval object.

### Example membership event

Something like:

AddMember(GroupID, Epoch, John_IK_pub, permissions, expiration, signed_by_admin)

All clients enforce this rule:

•           only accept John as a member if the add event has a valid admin signature

•           only send the next group key to John if that add event exists and is valid

That means Jane alone cannot add John, even if she wants to.

---

## Very important distinction

There are two different things:

### A. “Can Jane ask to add John?”

Yes.

### B. “Can Jane cause John to become a real member?”

Not without Bob’s admin signature.

That is the cryptographic separation you want.

---

## Recommended simple protocol structure

Here is a good simple implementation model.

# Entities

### Per user

•           Ed25519 identity signing keypair

•           X25519 encryption keypair

•           optional device keys if multi-device

### Per group

•           Group identifier

•           Group admin public key

•           Membership list

•           Current epoch

•           Current group key for that epoch

### Queue

The queue is untrusted storage and transport. It can: - store ciphertext - order messages approximately or append-only - serve history

It should **not** need to know plaintext or secrets.

---

## Message types in the queue

Define explicit message types.

### 1. Chat message

Posted by any valid member.

Contains: - type = CHAT - group id - epoch - sender id/public key reference - encrypted payload under current group key - sender signature

Rule: - must be from a valid member of that epoch - must verify signature - must decrypt under that epoch key

---

### 2. Invite request

Posted by Jane if she wants John added.

Contains: - type = INVITE_REQUEST - group id - requester = Jane - candidate = John public keys - optional note/metadata - Jane signature

Rule: - does **not** make John a member - only records a request

---

### 3. Admin approval / Add member

Posted by Bob.

Contains: - type = ADD_MEMBER - group id - new member = John - effective epoch = next epoch - Bob admin signature

Rule: - this is the first event that actually changes membership

---

### 4. Rekey event

Posted by Bob, or generated by admin policy.

Contains: - type = REKEY - old epoch - new epoch - for each allowed member, a copy of the new group key encrypted to that member’s public key - admin signature

Rule: - everyone moves to new epoch - removed users do not receive the new group key

This is how kicks and secure membership changes work.

---

### 5. Kick member

Contains: - type = REMOVE_MEMBER - target = Jane - effective next epoch - admin signature

Usually in practice, **kick and rekey happen together**.

Because removing someone is meaningless unless you also change the group key.

---

## The most important cryptographic idea in your system

Because your queue keeps old encrypted messages forever, **membership control is really key-distribution control**.

In other words:

•           if someone has the epoch key, they can read that epoch

•           if they do not have the epoch key, they cannot

So: - adding someone means securely giving them the new epoch key - kicking someone means rotating to a new epoch key and **not** giving it to them

That is the heart of the whole design.

---

## How to model Jane, Bob, and John

## Jane

Jane should have: - identity private/public key - device encryption keypair if needed - current authorized group epoch keys for groups she belongs to

Jane should **not** need Bob’s admin key.

She can: - send chat messages - request actions - read messages for epochs she has keys for

She cannot: - change membership by herself - issue authoritative rekeys - approve invites unless protocol explicitly allows delegated admin

---

## Bob

Bob has: - identity keys - group membership like everyone else - admin signing key for the group

He can: - approve joins - kick members - change policy - rotate group keys - perform full queue reset

---

## John

John initially has: - his own identity keys only

He becomes a valid member only after: - Bob’s signed approval exists - John receives the current or next epoch group key encrypted to him

---

## About your “master key + GC key” idea

Your concept is close, but I would rename things so the roles are clearer.

### Better naming

Instead of: - master private key - GC key - admin key

Use: - **identity key** = proves who the user is - **group epoch key** = decrypts messages for a given epoch - **admin authorization key** = approves privileged actions

That avoids confusion because “master key” often suggests one key controlling everything, which can get dangerous fast.

---

## How invites should work

Here is a simple secure invite flow.

## Option A, strict admin-only add

This sounds closest to what you want.

### Flow

1.         Jane posts INVITE_REQUEST(John_pub)

2.         Bob reviews it

3.         Bob posts ADD_MEMBER(John_pub) signed with admin key

4.         Bob or the group posts REKEY(epoch N -> N+1)

5.         new group key is encrypted separately to:

–          Bob

–          Jane

–          all remaining members

–          John

Now John can read from epoch N+1 onward.

### Security property

Jane cannot bypass Bob because clients will reject any member addition that lacks Bob’s admin signature.

---

## Option B, admin-issued invite tokens

If you want Jane to be able to “carry” permission from Bob, then Bob can issue Jane a limited capability.

Example: - Bob signs a token saying Jane may invite one user before date X

Then Jane can use that token to add someone.

This is called a **capability** approach.

That is useful if you want delegation, but for your first implementation I recommend **not** doing this yet. Start simpler with direct admin approval.

---

## How kicks should work

For a kick, you need more than just a signed kick message.

You need:

1.         REMOVE_MEMBER(Jane) signed by Bob

2.         new epoch key GK_N+1

3.         key distribution only to remaining members

4.         all future messages encrypted under GK_N+1

That gives you: - Jane can still read old epochs she already had - Jane cannot read future messages

That is the best you can do in a system that stores past encrypted history.

You generally **cannot make someone forget old keys** they already had.

So no cryptography can stop a kicked member from reading history they already legitimately received.

It can only stop future access.

---

## How “change everyone’s encryption keys” should work

This is just a **full rekey** or **epoch reset**.

Bob posts: - RESET_GROUP_CRYPTO - new epoch - fresh group key - fresh member key envelopes for every still-authorized user - admin signature

Optional stronger version: - also rotate per-sender ratchets or chain keys - reissue member credentials - invalidate old pending invites

This is a good admin function.

---

## A practical implementation path

If you want **simple technology**, I would suggest this stack.

## Identity and signatures

•           **Ed25519** for signatures

Use for: - user identity signing - admin authorization signing - queue event authenticity

---

## Key exchange / wrapping keys to members

•           **X25519** for public-key key agreement

Use for: - encrypting new epoch keys to each member individually - onboarding a new member - sending rekey material

---

## Symmetric message encryption

•           **XChaCha20-Poly1305**

Use for: - encrypting actual chat payloads - encrypting stored queue message bodies

Why: - simpler nonce story than standard ChaCha20-Poly1305 - very good for distributed systems - libsodium supports it nicely

---

## Recommended library

For a simpler implementation: - **libsodium / NaCl** - or language bindings based on it

This gives you: - modern primitives - fewer footguns - simpler APIs than assembling low-level primitives manually

If you are implementing in: - Rust: libsodium-sys, sodiumoxide, or modern Rust crypto crates - Go: golang.org/x/crypto plus a careful design - Java/Kotlin: Tink or libsodium bindings - JS/TS: libsodium wrappers - Python: PyNaCl

If your goal is “simple and sane,” **libsodium-style design is probably best**.

---

## What the queue server should and should not do

## The queue server can

•           accept append-only encrypted items

•           assign IDs or timestamps

•           replicate storage

•           serve history

•           maybe enforce anti-spam or quotas

## The queue server should not need to

•           know plaintext

•           generate trust decisions

•           decide who is a member by itself

•           hold private group secrets

Membership truth should come from **signed protocol events**, not server trust.

---

## Suggested data model

Each queue item should be an authenticated object like:

•           message type

•           group id

•           epoch

•           sender id

•           previous hash or monotonic counter if you want integrity chaining

•           payload

•           signature

You may also want: - event_id - created_at - device_id - parent_event_id for admin changes or invite workflows

This helps with auditability and replay protection.

---

## Important security properties to aim for

## 1. Authentication

Every action is signed by the actor’s identity key.

## 2. Authorization

Privileged actions are accepted only if signed by the admin key.

## 3. Confidentiality

Chat payloads are encrypted under the current epoch group key.

## 4. Forward membership control

Kicked users cannot read future epochs.

## 5. History retention

Old messages remain stored, but only users with old keys can decrypt them.

## 6. Replay protection

Messages/events should carry counters, IDs, or hashes so old events cannot be maliciously replayed as new ones.

---

## Where your design can go wrong if you are not careful

## 1. Sharing private master keys

This weakens identity and accountability badly.

## 2. One key doing too many jobs

Do not use one private key for: - identity - encryption - admin authorization all at once.

Separate these roles.

## 3. No epoch system

If membership changes without rekeying, kicked users still read everything.

## 4. Letting the server define membership

That makes the system trust the server too much.

## 5. No signed admin events

Then “admin approval” becomes policy only, not cryptographic enforcement.

---

## The simplest secure rule set

If you want a compact version of the whole protocol, I would define these rules:

### Rule 1

Every user has a permanent identity keypair.

### Rule 2

Every group has: - admin public key - member list - current epoch - current group key

### Rule 3

Every chat message must: - be signed by sender identity key - be encrypted with current epoch group key

### Rule 4

Every membership change must: - be signed by admin key - trigger a new epoch key

### Rule 5

Every new epoch key must be encrypted separately to each authorized member.

### Rule 6

Clients accept only admin-signed membership events as authoritative.

That already gives you a clean and defensible protocol skeleton.

---

## Summary in plain English

Your idea is workable if you split power correctly:

•           **user identity key** = I am Jane

•           **group key** = I can read/send messages in this chat right now

•           **admin key** = I am allowed to approve membership and force rekeys

So:

•           Jane can talk because she has the current group key

•           Jane can prove she is Jane because she has her identity key

•           Jane cannot add John by herself because clients require Bob’s admin signature for membership changes

•           Bob can kick people by issuing a signed remove event and rotating the group key

•           Bob can reset the chat cryptography by creating a fresh epoch and redistributing keys only to authorized users

That is the cleanest way to make your cryptography match your intended permissions.

If you build version 1, I would use:

•           **Ed25519** for signatures

•           **X25519** for key agreement / wrapping group keys to members

•           **XChaCha20-Poly1305** for message encryption

•           **append-only signed event log** for queue state

•           **epoch-based rekeying** for add/kick/reset

That is simple, modern, and fits your architecture well.

## One final note

What you are describing starts to resemble: - secure group messaging - append-only event logs - capability-based authorization - MLS-style group rekey ideas

You do **not** need to implement full MLS complexity to get started, but you should borrow its core insight: **membership changes must be tied to group key changes.**

Great project idea — what you’re describing is very achievable, and it actually maps closely onto known constructions (SimpleX’s SMP queues, Signal’s “sender keys,” and MLS-style group rekeying). Let me walk through the theory, then draw you the diagrams.

I’ll make two reasonable assumptions (tell me if either is wrong and I’ll adjust): the **queue server is untrusted** (it stores ciphertext and verifies signatures, but can never read content), and by “master key” you mean each user’s **long-term identity keypair**.

## The key model (4 key types)

**1. Master key (per user, asymmetric)** — e.g., an Ed25519 signing keypair + X25519 encryption keypair. This is the user’s identity. The private half signs every message they post; the public half is what others use to verify authorship and to encrypt secrets _to_ them.

**2. GC key / queue key (shared, symmetric)** — e.g., an XChaCha20-Poly1305 key. This is what actually encrypts message content in the queue. Critically, it’s **versioned by epoch**: GC key #1, #2, #3… Every rekey event bumps the epoch.

**3. Admin key (Bob only, asymmetric)** — an Ed25519 keypair whose _public_ half is baked into the queue’s metadata at creation time. It’s the **root of trust** for the whole GC. Nothing about membership is valid unless it carries a signature from this key.

**4. Membership credential (the glue)** — this is the piece that gives you what you asked for: _“Jane cannot invite John without Bob.”_ A credential is simply:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The server (and every member) rejects any queue write that doesn’t carry a credential verifiable under Bob’s admin public key. Jane physically **cannot forge** this for John — that’s the unforgeability property of digital signatures. She can _request_ it, but only Bob’s private admin key can mint it. That’s your cryptographic enforcement, not just a server rule.

## How the core flows work

•           **Sending:** Jane encrypts her message with the current epoch’s GC key (AEAD), signs the ciphertext with her master private key, attaches her credential, and appends to the queue. The queue verifies (credential valid? epoch current? signature matches?) and stores the ciphertext **forever** (your persistence twist — the server still learns nothing).

•           **Reading:** Any member pulls ciphertexts, verifies the sender’s signature + credential, decrypts with the GC key. Because messages are kept, a new member given older epoch keys can read history; give them only the current key and history stays sealed.

•           **Invite (request-to-join):** Jane posts a signed _join-request_ control message containing John’s master public key → Bob approves by (a) signing a credential for John and (b) encrypting the current GC key to John’s public key (a “sealed box”). Without step (b), John can’t read; without (a), the queue won’t accept his writes.

•           **Kick / full rekey:** Bob posts a signed _rekey_ control message: new epoch number + the new GC key individually encrypted to **each remaining member’s** master public key. The kicked user’s credential is revoked (epoch bump invalidates it) and they never receive the new key — cryptographically deaf and mute from that point on.

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Great project idea — this is very achievable with well-understood cryptography, and your instincts map almost perfectly onto how real systems (Signal groups, MLS, SimpleX) do it. Let me explain the theory, name your keys properly, show what tech to use, and draw you a diagram.

## Mapping your idea to real cryptography

Your four key types correspond to standard primitives:

|Your term|Crypto equivalent|Purpose|
|---|---|---|
|**Master private key**|Long-term identity keypair (Ed25519 sign + X25519 encrypt)|Proves _who_ is speaking; signs every message; receives encrypted key material|
|**GC / queue key**|Shared symmetric group key (e.g. XChaCha20-Poly1305 key), per “epoch”|Encrypts/decrypts actual message content in the queue|
|**Admin key**|A distinct signing keypair whose public half is baked into the queue’s metadata at creation|Authorizes control operations (invite, kick, rekey)|
|**Public keys**|Public halves of the above|Distributed openly so others can verify signatures and encrypt things _to_ you|

The core principle that makes your whole design work is: **the queue server never sees plaintext, but it _does_ verify signatures on control messages.** Content privacy comes from encryption; admin authority comes from signatures.

## How each requirement works

**1. Sending & reading messages (Jane)** - Jane encrypts her message with the current **group key** (epoch key), then **signs the ciphertext with her master key**. - She appends it to the queue. Every member fetches it, verifies her signature against her known public master key, and decrypts with the same group key. - Because you _keep_ messages instead of deleting them, the queue is an **append-only encrypted log** — new members can even be given old epoch keys if you want history sharing, or denied them for forward secrecy. That’s a design choice you control per-epoch.

**2. Invites require Bob’s approval (the part you asked about)** This is done with **admin-signed membership credentials** — essentially mini-certificates: - Jane sends an _invite request_ into the queue (or a side channel): “I propose John, here’s John’s public master key,” signed by Jane. - Bob’s client sees it and, if he approves, signs a **membership credential**: sign(admin_key, {John_pubkey, queue_id, epoch, permissions, expiry}). - The queue server **refuses any join/read/write from a key that doesn’t present a valid admin-signed credential.** The server only needs Bob’s admin _public_ key to verify — it never holds any secret. - Cryptographically, Jane _cannot_ forge this: she can’t produce a valid signature under Bob’s admin key. So “request to join” is enforced by math, not policy. - To actually let John read, Bob (or an authorized member, post-approval) encrypts the current group key **to John’s public master key** and posts it as a “welcome” control message.

**3. Kicking + resetting all cryptography (rekey)** This is the classic **epoch rotation** pattern: - Bob posts an admin-signed control message: “Epoch N ends. Member X removed.” - Bob generates a fresh group key for epoch N+1 and encrypts a copy **individually to each remaining member’s public master key** (X25519 sealed box per member). The kicked member’s key gets nothing. - All new messages use the new epoch key. The kicked user can still hold old ciphertexts but can’t read anything new — that’s **post-compromise security via rekeying**. - The server also revokes the kicked member’s credential so they can’t even fetch new queue entries.

For small groups (< ~100 people), “encrypt the new key to everyone individually” is totally fine — it’s O(n) and simple. Only at large scale do you need tree-based schemes like MLS’s TreeKEM.

**4. Bob’s admin key itself** Bob is just a regular member (master + group key) _plus_ the admin keypair. The queue is created with the admin public key pinned in its metadata, so authority is bound to the queue itself, not to Bob’s account. (Bonus: this lets Bob hand off admin by signing a “new admin key” control message.)

## Simple technology stack to implement this

•           **libsodium** (or PyNaCl / sodium bindings in any language) — gives you everything: Ed25519 signatures, X25519 sealed boxes, XChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD, and key generation. This is genuinely all you need.

•           **HKDF** for deriving epoch keys / per-message subkeys from the group key.

•           **Server**: any append-only store — even SQLite/Postgres with an INSERT-only table of (queue_id, seq, ciphertext, sender_sig) behind a WebSocket or HTTP long-poll. The server logic is just: _verify credential → verify signature → append → fan out_.

•           **If you want a battle-tested protocol instead of rolling your own**: **MLS (RFC 9420)**, implemented by **OpenMLS** (Rust). It literally is “group chat with epochs, admin-controlled adds/removes, and rekeying” — your design is a simplified MLS. SimpleX itself, and Signal’s _sender keys_, are also good references to read.

•           For message signing format: **libsodium detached signatures** or PASETO if you want structured tokens for the credentials.

⚠️ One rule: don’t invent primitives — only invent the _composition_ (which you’ve basically done correctly). Use libsodium’s constructions as-is.

Great concept — this is very buildable, and the good news is you don’t need to invent new cryptography. What you’re describing maps cleanly onto three well-understood primitives: **signatures for identity, admin-signed credentials for authorization, and epoch-based symmetric keys for the group secret**. Here’s the full picture.

## How the keys work together

![](data:image/png;base64,)

**The four key types and their real cryptographic roles:**

•           **Master key (per user)** — This is an asymmetric _identity keypair_ (e.g., Ed25519 for signing + X25519 for receiving encrypted material). Jane’s master private key proves “this message really came from Jane” and lets her _receive_ wrapped group keys. It never touches message content directly.

•           **GC key (shared, per epoch)** — This is a _symmetric_ key (e.g., ChaCha20-Poly1305) that actually encrypts messages. Everyone in the group holds the current one. Critically, it’s **versioned by epoch** (v1, v2, v3…) — this is what makes kicks and resets work.

•           **Admin key (Bob only)** — Another asymmetric signing keypair, but it’s the **root of trust** for the queue. The queue server is configured at creation time to only honor control actions (add member, kick, rekey) that carry a valid signature from this key.

•           **Public keys** — Everyone’s master _public_ keys are known to the group and the queue. They’re used to verify signatures and to wrap (encrypt) GC keys to specific people.

## The trick that makes admin permission cryptographically mandatory

This is the heart of your question. The answer is **membership credentials**:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Every write to the queue must include a credential signed by Bob’s admin key. The queue verifies two things before appending anything: the message signature (proves _who_ sent it) and the credential (proves _the admin authorized this person_). Since signatures are unforgeable without the private key, **Jane mathematically cannot mint a credential for John** — she can send Bob a signed _invite request_ into the queue, but until Bob produces cred_John, the queue rejects everything John submits, and John never receives the GC key anyway (only Bob can wrap it to him). Two independent locks, both requiring Bob.

## Message flow, invites, and kick/rekey in action

![](data:image/png;base64,)

**Normal send:** Jane encrypts with the current GC key, signs with her master key, attaches her credential → queue verifies and appends → everyone fetches and decrypts. The server stores ciphertext forever but can never read it.

**Kick + full crypto reset (Bob’s admin functions):** Bob posts a signed Kick(jane_pub) + Rekey control message. The queue immediately revokes Jane’s credential. Bob then generates gc_key_v2 and wraps it individually to each _remaining_ member’s master public key (this is HPKE / libsodium “sealed boxes”). Jane still holds v1, so she can read old history she already had — but everything after the epoch bump is opaque to her. This is exactly the “change everyone’s encryption keys” reset you wanted, and it’s cheap: one wrap per member.

## Recommended technology stack (simple → robust)

•           **libsodium** (or PyNaCl / sodium bindings in any language) — gives you Ed25519 signatures, X25519 sealed boxes, and XChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD in a hard-to-misuse package. This alone covers ~90% of your protocol.

•           **HPKE (RFC 9180)** — the standardized way to wrap the GC key to each member’s public key, if you want something more formal than sealed boxes.

•           **Signal’s “Sender Keys”** pattern — your GC-key-per-epoch design is essentially this; worth reading as prior art (it’s how WhatsApp groups work).

•           **MLS (RFC 9420, e.g., OpenMLS library)** — the heavyweight option. It gives you tree-based group key agreement with efficient rekeys at scale (log n instead of n wraps) plus forward secrecy and post-compromise security built in. Overkill for a prototype, ideal for production.

•           **Queue transport** — since you’re SimpleX-inspired: an append-only log per group (even something as simple as a server holding ordered blobs) works. The server needs zero knowledge of content; it only verifies Ed25519 signatures and credentials.

## Summary

Your intuition is sound and the design decomposes into: **(1)** master keys = identity + key-receiving, **(2)** a shared symmetric GC key per epoch = actual message encryption, **(3)** an admin key whose signatures act as unforgeable permission slips (credentials) that gate every privileged action. Invites without Bob are impossible because members can’t forge his signature and can’t wrap the GC key to outsiders through the queue’s enforcement; kicks/resets are just “revoke credential + bump epoch + redistribute key.” One honest caveat since you keep messages forever: a stored-forever encrypted log weakens forward secrecy (a leaked epoch key exposes that whole epoch’s history), so rekeying _periodically_ — not just on kicks — is a cheap way to limit blast radius.

Happy to go deeper on any piece — e.g., the exact credential format, how the queue validates writes, or a small libsodium proof-of-concept in Python.

Your design is sound and actually maps very closely to how real-world secure group messaging already works. Let me explain it in proper cryptographic terms, then give you the diagram and concrete tech.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Translating your idea into standard crypto primitives

Your intuition is right, but the trick is that **each of your “keys” is really a keypair or a symmetric secret with a specific job**:

**1. Master key (per user, e.g. Jane)** → a long-term **identity keypair** (e.g. Ed25519 for signing + X25519 for key exchange). The private half never leaves her device. Its jobs: - **Sign** every message she posts, so members can verify “this really came from Jane.” - **Receive secrets**: others can encrypt things _to_ her using her public half (this is how she gets the group key).

**2. GC key (queue key)** → a **shared symmetric group key** (e.g. an AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 key). Everyone in the group holds the same one for the current “epoch.” Its job: encrypt/decrypt the actual message contents. The server storing the queue never has it, so your persisted queue stays opaque forever — which fits your “keep messages instead of deleting” model nicely.

**3. Admin key (Bob)** → a second **signing keypair** whose public half is baked into the queue’s metadata at creation. The server (and all clients) treat it as the **root of authority**: any control operation — add member, kick, rekey — is only valid if it carries a signature verifiable against Bob’s admin public key.

## How this makes admin approval _cryptographically_ enforced

This is the part you asked about: how do we make it _impossible_ (not just “against the rules”) for Jane to add John?

Membership is defined by a **signed credential**, not by knowing keys. To post to or read the queue, a client must present a credential like:

“User with public key PK_John is a member of group G during epoch N” — **signed by the admin key**.

•           Jane physically **cannot forge** that signature (that’s the whole security guarantee of Ed25519). She can send Bob a signed _invite request_ through the queue, but only Bob can mint the credential.

•           Even if Jane leaks the current group key to John, John can’t _post_ (the server rejects uncredentialed writes) and he gets locked out of reading anything new the moment Bob rotates the key. Wilful key-leaking is the “simulate someone else as her” case you said you’re not worried about — correct, no cryptography can stop that.

## Kick + full rekey (epoch rotation)

This is the standard pattern:

1.         Bob posts an admin-signed control message: _“Epoch N ends; member X removed.”_

2.         Bob generates a fresh group key for **epoch N+1**.

3.         He encrypts (“seals”) that new key **individually to each remaining member’s public master key** and posts those sealed packets to the queue.

4.         Kicked user X can still decrypt old epoch-N history they already had (unavoidable — they had the key), but everything from epoch N+1 onward is unreadable to them. This property is called **forward-looking access revocation / post-compromise security**.

Since your queue is persistent, a nice bonus: new members like John can be granted either **only the current epoch key** (no history) or older epoch keys too (full history) — Bob controls history visibility per-invite. That’s a feature SimpleX can’t offer because it deletes.

## Simple technologies to build this with

|Job|Recommended primitive|Easy library|
|---|---|---|
|Identity/master keypairs|Ed25519 (sign) + X25519 (exchange)|**libsodium / PyNaCl**|
|Message encryption (GC key)|XChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-256-GCM|libsodium secretbox|
|Sealing group key to a member|libsodium **sealed boxes** (crypto_box_seal)|PyNaCl SealedBox|
|Admin credentials|Ed25519 signatures over (member pubkey, group ID, epoch, expiry)|PyNaCl SigningKey|
|Key derivation / epochs|HKDF ratcheting the group key each epoch|cryptography lib HKDF|
|Queue transport|Any append-only log: Redis Streams, NATS JetStream, Kafka, or plain SQLite/Postgres table|—|

If you later want to scale to large groups with efficient rekeys (rekey cost log(n) instead of n), the “grown-up” version of this exact design is **MLS (Messaging Layer Security, RFC 9420)** — libraries: OpenMLS (Rust). But for a first implementation, **libsodium + sender-signs / group-key-encrypts / admin-signs-credentials** is genuinely enough and much simpler.

## Summary of message flow (matches the diagram)

1.         **Send**: Jane encrypts plaintext with the epoch-N group key, signs the ciphertext with her master private key, attaches her admin-signed credential, appends to the queue.

2.         **Receive**: members pull, check her credential (admin sig), verify her signature (her public master key), decrypt with the group key.

3.         **Invite**: Jane posts a signed _request_; Bob approves by minting John’s credential and sealing the group key to John’s public master key. Without Bob, mathematically no valid credential can exist.

4.         **Kick/rekey**: Bob signs an epoch-end control message and distributes a fresh group key to survivors only.

One design decision worth thinking about early: do you want the **server** to enforce credentials on write (spam protection, but the server learns membership metadata), or purely **client-side** verification (server learns less, but bad writes land in the queue and get discarded by readers)? Most systems do both. Also decide whether “change everyone’s keys” resets _history_ access or just future access — with a persistent queue those are meaningfully different.
